rv.q: I left the show with the feeling the playwright's work is always capable of delivering in good hands: buzzy, wide awake, like my brain had been washed in seltzer.

The Map has managed something rather wonderful: it has made an intimidating work feel intimate, made scholarship feel sensual, and made a dead poet’s inability to say what he wanted to say feel, after all these years, like something we can hear.
The truly crucial point is that this early in the 2026-27 season, a production setting a high bar has already arrived.
Director Zachary Lindsay’s small-scale staging is just as moving and elegant.
The ideas fly by fast and furious, each more interesting than the last, and days later I’m still thinking about it.
This Invention proves that even a quasi‑biographical snapshot of an esteemed literary lion, at its essence, can (and should) be relatable to each and every audience member.
I recommend it for anyone who loves the work of words and seeing a show that holds the human being in high regard as an intellect and a creature who loves, and loves deeply.

In this rare revival, Zachary Elkind’s direction and David Greenspan’s mesmerizing performance transform Housman’s final journey into a poignant meditation on love, memory, and the price of keeping desire hidden.
His production, like the play, is an impressive achievement.

This latest revival of The Invention of Love doesn't solve the play's lack of emotional catharsis but it's always nice to luxuriate in Stoppard's words, especially when it's tackled with the ferocity that the great David Greenspan provides here—not to be missed.
Direction (Anothony Elkind) makes brilliant use of the space creating movement and variation that never seems extraneous.
Unfortunately, at nearly three hours, Stoppard seems determined to give us all of them at once.
You don't have to be a Classics major to fall under the magical spell of The Invention of Love.

cn.t: Critics praise this rare Stoppard revival as intellectually rich and deeply moving, anchored by David Greenspan's luminous performance as A.E. Housman and Zachary Elkind's sharp direction that transforms dense material into exquisite theater.

vr.q: There's a lot to take away from this compelling piece, but whether it's compelling as a play is more of a debate.

I question if this was the right play for them to pick under the circumstances. But at the same time, clearly no one else is stepping up to the plate to revive this play. And I do think it's worth reviving.
